design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis (inverse variance, Hedges' g) of neurocognitive performance in people who had used MDMA recreationally and had been abstinent from it for at least 6 months, compared with people still using MDMA (at least 7 days since last use) and with MDMA-naive comparison groups. 14 studies included (11 cross-sectional case-control studies, 3 prospective cohorts); 5 entered a meta-analysis of learning and memory; the other domains (executive function, complex attention, language, perceptual-motor) were summarized narratively by DSM-5 neurocognitive domain. Protocol on the Open Science Framework, registered 18 March 2023 and revised 30 November 2023. Published online 2025, issue 2026.
can_establish: How people abstinent from MDMA for at least 6 months compared with people still using it and with MDMA-naive comparison groups on learning and memory tests in the studies published up to August 2024, and how few and how heterogeneous those studies are.
cannot_establish: That MDMA caused the lower scores or that scores do not recover after stopping (the comparisons are between different people, mostly at one time point, with no measure before use); whether longer abstinence helps (the authors did not test it, p. 279); or the size of any effect in a defined population (4 or 5 studies per estimate with heterogeneity of 80 to 96%).

sample.recruitment: Database search (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane, Web of Science, PsycINFO, CINAHL) from inception to 9 August 2024, developed with a hospital librarian, plus reference lists of included articles (Material and methods › Search strategy, p. 274; Table 1, p. 275). 8172 records, 5631 after removing duplicates, 214 sought, 213 assessed in full, 14 included; 3 more from citation searching all excluded (Figure 1, p. 275). Studies came from the UK (7), the Netherlands, Australia and Germany (2 each) and Canada (1) (Results › Study characteristics, p. 276).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: humans who used MDMA recreationally with a group abstinent from MDMA for at least 6 months; any current-use comparison group at least 7 days after last use; standardized neurocognitive tests; peer-reviewed publications only; all languages eligible. Excluded: studies where MDMA was given with another substance or medication, and global cognitive screening tools (pp. 275-276). Excluded full texts by reason in Figure 1: acute effects or washout under 7 days 72, no group abstinent more than 6 months 72, non-standardized tool 18, abstract only 17, unclear abstinence 10, others 10 (p. 275).
sample.demographics: Table 2 (pp. 277-278): group sizes from 3 to 182; mean ages mostly in the twenties; mean lifetime use above 100 tablets in 9 studies (up to 500 to 600 in some) and below 100 in 1; minimum abstinence 6 months in 8 studies, 12 months in 1, 18 months in 2, 24 months in 2 and 48 months in 1 (pp. 276, 279).
sample.selection_effects: Peer-reviewed publications only, with no grey literature or registry search; the evidence is weighted towards UK case-control studies, four of them by the same first author with the same abstinent participants (p. 280). In every study the current and abstinent MDMA groups had used other drugs; most comparison groups had too, and only one study, the largest, had a completely drug-naive comparison group (pp. 276, 279).

exposure.measurement: As reported by the primary studies: mean lifetime tablets in almost all, a range only in one, a minimum in another, no quantity in one (p. 276); the review notes reliance on self-report for exposure in 12 of the 14 studies (p. 279).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: No dose-response analysis, because most participants would be classified as having heavy use (more than 100 lifetime tablets) and the study with the lowest exposure (36 to 69 tablets on average) also had the longest abstinence (p. 282).
exposure.polysubstance: All current and abstinent MDMA groups had histories of other drug use; most comparison groups did as well; two studies used comparison groups using only alcohol and tobacco and one (Taurah et al., 2014; 154, 157 and 182 people) a completely drug-naive group (pp. 276, 279; Table 2). Not addressed in the meta-analysis, which pooled unadjusted group means; the authors list polysubstance use as a limitation and note that the comparison groups' drug use was often much lower (p. 282).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Abstinent groups at least 6 months by inclusion; current-use groups at least 7 days since last use (p. 275). Minimum periods by study as above (p. 279).

comparison.controls: MDMA-naive comparison groups, mostly people who used other drugs; people still using MDMA as a second comparison.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level; the appraisal found concerns about matching in all case-control studies and about comparability of abstinent and control groups in all studies (p. 279).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No included study measured cognition before MDMA use began; the authors raise pre-existing characteristics such as trait impulsivity as a possible explanation for differences (p. 282).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Mostly yes (polysubstance comparison groups); none in the largest meta-analysed study.

outcomes.instruments: Standardized neuropsychological tests classified by a clinical neuropsychologist into DSM-5 neurocognitive domains (learning and memory, executive function, complex attention, language, perceptual-motor, social cognition); the classification is in Supplemental Appendix A-1 (not read) (p. 276).
outcomes.validity_norms: Primary-study quality rated by two independent raters with the Joanna Briggs Institute checklists for case-control and cohort studies, plus a global rating of poor or fair (p. 276); all 3 cohorts and 6 of 11 case-control studies poor, 5 case-control studies fair (p. 279). Item-level ratings are in Supplemental Appendix B (not read).
outcomes.operationalization: Pooled standardized mean differences (Hedges' g) between groups for overall learning and memory and for verbal and visual immediate and delayed memory; how several measures from one study were combined into the overall estimate is not described.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 11 counts the pooled estimates in Table 3 (p. 280).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Screening of titles, abstracts and full texts by two independent reviewers with a third for disagreements (p. 274); quality rated by two independent raters (p. 276); whether data extraction was done by one or two people is not described (p. 276).

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 3 (p. 280), Hedges' g with 95% CI and I2. Current vs abstinent: overall 0.03 (-0.35 to 0.41), 5 studies, I2 79.77%; verbal immediate 0.00 (-0.46 to 0.47), 4 studies, I2 36.89%; verbal delayed 0.24 (-1.17 to 1.66), 4 studies, I2 92.23%; visual immediate -0.01 (-0.49 to 0.47), 2 studies, I2 14.79%; visual delayed -0.17 (-0.62 to 0.27), 2 studies, I2 0%. Abstinent vs MDMA-naive: overall -1.37 (-2.65 to -0.09), 4 studies, I2 96.02%; verbal immediate -1.22 (-3.63 to 1.18), 3 studies, I2 94.18%; verbal delayed -1.30 (-4.15 to 1.54), 3 studies, I2 95.54%. Current vs MDMA-naive: overall -1.06 (-1.98 to -0.15), 4 studies, I2 94.58%; verbal immediate -0.41 (-0.88 to 0.06), 3 studies, I2 28.37%; verbal delayed -1.16 (-2.58 to 0.26), 3 studies, I2 90.45%. Sensitivity analysis without the poor-quality cohort: the current vs abstinent result unchanged (p. 279). No tau-squared, prediction intervals or study weights are given in the article (forest plots are in Supplemental Appendices C and D, not read).
analysis.covariates: None at review level; unadjusted group means were pooled.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Open Science Framework protocol registered 18 March 2023 and revised 30 November 2023 (p. 274); the reference list gives its title as a systematic review (revised protocol) (p. 285). The protocol was not read, so whether the meta-analysis and an analysis by length of abstinence were planned, and any deviations, could not be checked; the article reports no deviations.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only learning and memory were pooled, the other domains being judged too heterogeneous (p. 276), although the pooled comparisons with MDMA-naive groups have I2 of 95 to 96%. The planned contrast of longer abstinence was not done (p. 279), yet its result is stated in the abstract and conclusion (pp. 273, 282). Publication bias was not assessed.
analysis.power: Not addressed. 2 to 5 studies per estimate; some groups very small (an abstinent group of 3 in Morgan, 1999; Table 2, p. 277).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 4 heterogeneous studies, both current and abstinent groups scored lower than MDMA-naive groups on overall learning and memory (g -1.06 and -1.37, with intervals reaching -0.15 and -0.09 and I2 of 95 and 96%); every verbal-memory subtest interval included zero; and abstinent groups did not differ from current groups (g 0.03, -0.35 to 0.41). Executive function, attention, language and perceptual-motor results could not be pooled and were mostly null or inconsistent; the 3 small cohorts, all of poor quality, disagreed.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusion state that a longer period of abstinence did not demonstrate greater improvement or recovery (pp. 273, 282), but the Results say that the effect of longer abstinence beyond 6 months was not tested (p. 279). The Results say the verbal subcategory analyses showed both abstinent and current groups performing "significantly more poorly" than MDMA-naive controls (p. 279), while every one of these intervals in Table 3 includes zero (p. 280). The Discussion reads the cross-sectional comparison of different people as showing that 6 months of abstinence is insufficient for people who have stopped to reach naive-level performance (p. 282), and argues that learning and memory changes are specific to MDMA, a comparison the review did not make. Against this, the authors state that their results do not confirm permanent damage or that it is due to neurotoxic effects of MDMA, that the findings are of low quality, and that pre-existing differences could explain them (pp. 273, 282).

timeline.event: Cited for reduced CSF 5-HIAA (with a 1999 study by the same group, not read) and as indirect human evidence of dopamine-system damage (pp. 274, 281).

Earlier meta-analyses described in the introduction (Verbaten, 2003; Laws and Kokkalis, 2007; Kalechstein et al., 2007; Zakzanis et al., 2007; Nulsen et al., 2010; Roberts et al., 2016) report poorer memory, most consistently verbal, in people who use MDMA; none restricted to sustained abstinence (pp. 273-274; not read).
Prospective study of people starting ecstasy use cited as reporting impairment after light use (p. 282).

Muller et al. meta-analysis of 16 neuroimaging studies: lower serotonin transporter density in 8 of 13 regions, and a positive association with time abstinent that the review says rests largely on one small study (p. 281; not read).
This review: the first, by its authors' account, restricted to at least 6 months of abstinence (pp. 274, 282).

replication.where_it_stands: The review's learning-and-memory estimates rest on 4 or 5 studies with very high heterogeneity, and the authors call the findings low quality. Overlap with the earlier meta-analyses of the same cross-sectional literature was not assessed in the review and has not been checked here. The question of recovery with abstinence cannot be answered from cross-sectional comparisons between people who still use and people who have stopped.

funding.funder: The authors received no financial support for the research, authorship or publication (p. 283).
funding.affiliations_note: Metro North Mental Health (Queensland Health), the University of Queensland, West Moreton Hospital and Health Service, Queensland Centre for Mental Health Research and QIMR Berghofer (p. 273). Recorded as a flag for closer reading only.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts that test cognition before MDMA use and then repeatedly in people who continue and people who stop, with retested comparison groups, hair-verified exposure and abstinence, and an individual-participant analysis relating change in scores to time since stopping, against people who use the same other drugs.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (recreational MDMA use, at least 6 months abstinent), comparators (current use, MDMA-naive), outcomes (neurocognitive domains) stated (p. 275).

Open Science Framework protocol registered March 2023 and revised November 2023, before the search ended in August 2024; the protocol was not read, its cited title names a systematic review only, and no deviations are reported.
Case-control and cohort studies were included without an explanation of the choice of designs.

Six databases with a librarian-developed strategy (Table 1), reference lists, all languages, search within 24 months of publication; but the restriction to peer-reviewed publications is not justified and no grey literature, registries or experts were searched. Judged as written for unjustified publication restrictions (decision p-amstar2-item4); a lenient reading would give partial yes. The overall rating does not depend on this item.
Two authors independently screened titles, abstracts and full texts, with a third reviewer for discrepancies (p. 274).
Pre-defined extraction variables are listed, but who extracted the data, and whether two people did, is not described (p. 276).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Figure 1 gives the number of exclusions by reason; no list of excluded studies appears in the article, and none of the named supplements is described as holding one (supplements not read).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 2 gives design, group sizes, age, sex, MDMA use, comparison-group substance use, domains and minimum abstinence; setting, recruitment and the specific tests are not tabulated, and several entries are inconsistent (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: JBI checklists by two independent raters, covering confounding, matching and exposure measurement (p. 279); selection of the reported result is not covered; item-level ratings only in a supplement (not read).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Random-effects inverse-variance pooling of unadjusted group means from non-randomized studies, without justification for combining unadjusted data; pooled despite I2 of 95 to 96% with 4 studies, although high heterogeneity was the stated reason for not pooling the other domains; the handling of several measures per study in the overall estimate is not described; a cohort study was pooled with case-control studies without explanation.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: A sensitivity analysis excluding the only poor-quality study in the meta-analysis left the current vs abstinent result unchanged (p. 279); the comparisons with MDMA-naive groups contain only studies rated fair. Minimal, but it meets the item.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The abstract, critical appraisal and conclusion state that the findings are low quality and call for caution (pp. 273, 279, 282), and the limitations discuss confounding by other drug use and pre-existing traits (p. 282), although parts of the Discussion still overstate the results.
I2 is reported and heterogeneity in recruitment, populations, tests and confounding is named as a limitation (p. 282), but no subgroup, meta-regression or other investigation of its sources was done.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No funding and no conflicts declared (p. 283).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence because more than one critical item is not met: no list of excluded studies (item 7), pooling of unadjusted data with extreme heterogeneity (item 11) and no assessment of publication bias (item 15), and, as written, an unjustified restriction to peer-reviewed publications (item 4); items 2 and 9 are partly met and item 13 is met. This is a judgment about how far the pooled numbers can be trusted, not about the value of the question: the review is registered, searched widely without language limits, screened in duplicate and states its low certainty. Its pooled estimates should be read as describing a small, heterogeneous set of cross-sectional comparisons. It may be cited for those comparisons and for the absence of any analysis of longer abstinence; it may not be cited for recovery or its absence, or for a causal effect of MDMA.

key_findings.finding: 14 studies met the criteria (11 cross-sectional case-control, 3 prospective cohorts): 8 assessed learning and memory, 10 executive function, 5 complex attention, 2 language, 1 perceptual-motor function, none social cognition.

Learning and memory meta-analysis of 5 studies with, as stated, 228 people currently using MDMA, 218 abstinent at least 6 months and 229 MDMA-naive comparison participants; studies were left out for insufficient data (2) or participants already represented (1).
key_findings.note: Table 2 group sizes for the same 5 studies sum to 241, 208 and 231 (editors' arithmetic; the cohort study has no naive group); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Current vs abstinent (at least 6 months): no difference in overall learning and memory, g 0.03 (95% CI -0.35 to 0.41), 5 studies, I2 79.77%, unchanged when the poor-quality cohort was excluded; verbal and visual subtests also near zero (g -0.17 to 0.24, all intervals including zero).
key_findings.locator: Results › Learning and memory, 2nd paragraph (p. 279); Table 3 (p. 280)

key_findings.finding: Abstinent vs MDMA-naive: overall learning and memory g -1.37 (95% CI -2.65 to -0.09), 4 studies, I2 96.02%; current vs MDMA-naive: g -1.06 (-1.98 to -0.15), 4 studies, I2 94.58%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Learning and memory, 2nd paragraph (p. 279); Table 3 (p. 280)

key_findings.finding: Verbal memory subtests vs MDMA-naive groups: abstinent immediate -1.22 (-3.63 to 1.18) and delayed -1.30 (-4.15 to 1.54), 3 studies each, I2 94 to 96%; current immediate -0.41 (-0.88 to 0.06) and delayed -1.16 (-2.58 to 0.26). All four intervals include zero.
key_findings.note: The text says these subcategory analyses showed significantly poorer performance (p. 279); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Because of the small sample, the effect of longer durations of abstinence beyond 6 months was not tested.
key_findings.locator: Results › Learning and memory, 2nd paragraph (last sentence)

key_findings.finding: Of the three learning-and-memory studies not pooled, two case-control studies found impairment despite 12 to 24 months of abstinence, while a small 2-year prospective study of poor quality found memory improved in people who stopped and worsened in people who continued (Zakzanis and Campbell, 2006).

Executive function (10 studies): the two prospective studies (poor quality) found neither improvement nor deterioration after 18 months of abstinence; seven case-control studies found no significant difference between abstinent and MDMA-naive groups; four by the same author with the same abstinent participants showed a trend for abstinent groups to score between current-use groups and controls.
key_findings.locator: Results › Executive function, 1st paragraph (begins p. 279, continues p. 280)

key_findings.finding: Complex attention (5 cross-sectional studies): 4 of 5, including the largest, found no significant differences between current, abstinent and MDMA-naive groups; one found both MDMA groups poorer than controls on serial 7s. Language (2 studies) mixed; perceptual-motor (1 small study) a small improvement in people who stopped; social cognition no studies.
key_findings.locator: Results › Complex attention; Language; Perceptual motor function; Social cognition

key_findings.finding: Quality: all 3 cohorts and 6 of 11 case-control studies rated poor, 5 fair; comparability of abstinent and control groups questioned in all studies and matching in all case-control studies; exposure assessed by self-report in 12 of 14.

Polysubstance use: in all studies both MDMA groups had used other drugs; most comparison groups had too; two used alcohol- and tobacco-using controls, and only one (Taurah et al., 2014) a completely drug-naive comparison group.
key_findings.locator: Results › Patterns of MDMA use and other drug use, 1st paragraph (begins p. 276, continues p. 279)

key_findings.finding: Abstinence minima: 6 months in 8 studies, 12 months in 1, 18 months in 2, 24 months in 2, 48 months in 1; the study with the lowest exposure (mean 36 to 69 tablets) also had the longest abstinence, so dose and abstinence are confounded across studies; no dose-response analysis was done.
key_findings.locator: Results › Duration of abstinence (p. 279); Discussion, 6th paragraph (begins p. 281, continues p. 282)

key_findings.finding: The authors state that their results do not definitively confirm permanent damage or that it is due to neurotoxic effects of MDMA, that the conclusions rest on variable, low-quality findings, and that pre-existing traits may explain differences.

As summarized in the Discussion (studies not read): a meta-analysis of 16 neuroimaging studies found lower serotonin transporter density in 8 of 13 regions, with a positive association with time abstinent that rested largely on one small study (Muller et al., 2019); one study of people abstinent 2.5 years found possible transporter recovery without recovery of verbal memory (Thomasius et al., 2006).

reporting_issues.issue: The Results state that the verbal immediate and delayed subcategory analyses showed both abstinent and current MDMA groups performing significantly more poorly than MDMA-naive controls (p. 279), but all four intervals in Table 3 include zero (p. 280).
reporting_issues.consequence: The text overstates the subcategory results; only the overall estimates exclude zero, and only just.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and conclusion state that a longer period of abstinence did not demonstrate greater improvement or recovery (pp. 273, 282), but the Results say the effect of longer abstinence beyond 6 months was not tested (p. 279).
reporting_issues.consequence: A headline conclusion rests on an analysis that was not done; the only basis is the cross-sectional current vs abstinent comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: The meta-analysis totals do not add up: the text gives 228 current, 218 abstinent and 229 MDMA-naive participants in 5 studies and 74, 51 and 47 in the 4-study verbal subset (p. 279). Adding the largest study's Table 2 sizes (154, 157 and 182) to the subset gives 228 and 229 but 208, not 218; and Table 2's sizes for the four smaller studies sum to 87, 51 and 49 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of abstinent participants in the meta-analysis is uncertain (208 or 218).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 contains internal errors: in Taurah et al. (2014) the abstinent group is 66% men and 24% women, and in Ward et al. (2006) the current and comparison groups are 29% and 61%, and 23% and 67%, neither summing to 100; the abstinent group of Potter et al. (2013) is n = 17 but given as 4 men and 11 women with the same age as Morgan et al. (2002), whose row it appears to repeat.
reporting_issues.consequence: Study characteristics cannot be relied on without the primary papers.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2's entries for the Wareing studies differ from those printed by Murphy et al. (2009, Table 2), whose authors include the primary authors: the sample sizes and lifetime tablets given here for Wareing et al. (2004a, verbal working memory) and (2004b, visuospatial memory) are those Murphy et al. give for the other paper, and Wareing et al. (2005) has 291.33 lifetime tablets here vs 591.33 in Murphy et al.
reporting_issues.consequence: Likely transcription errors in this review; the primary studies have not been read, so which version is right is not settled.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results describe Zakzanis and Campbell (2006) as a 2-year study with findings at 18 months (pp. 279-280) and Table 2 gives its minimum abstinence as 24 months (p. 278); the language section reports vocabulary change at 18 months.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstinence and follow-up periods of this study are unclear from the review.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says Taurah et al. (2014) observed impairments in learning and memory and executive functioning that did not improve despite an average of 5 years of abstinence, and refers to no improvement up to 5 years of follow-up (pp. 281-282); Table 2 lists that study as cross-sectional and assessing learning and memory and complex attention only, and the executive-function section does not include it.
reporting_issues.consequence: A cross-sectional study is described as showing absence of improvement over time, and in a domain it did not assess.

reporting_issues.issue: The introduction cites McCann et al. (1994) as indirect human evidence of dopamine-system damage (p. 274); in that study the dopamine metabolite HVA was lower only in women and not on unequal-variance testing (card sc_mccann_1994).
reporting_issues.consequence: Overstatement of the dopamine evidence; not used in this review's analyses.

verification.source_read: PDF, pp. 273-285 (issue version, all pages; Figure 1, Table 2 and Table 3 checked on rendered pages; Supplemental Appendices A-D, including forest plots and item-level quality ratings, not read)
